clinicalPearls: Sandifer syndrome describes paroxysmal dystonic posturing — abnormal head and neck extension, torticollis and back arching (opisthotonus) — occurring in association with gastro-oesophageal reflux and, less commonly, hiatus hernia.
Episodes characteristically cluster around or shortly after feeds and abate during sleep, a temporal pattern that helps distinguish them from epileptic seizures.
Consciousness is fully preserved throughout episodes and there is no post-ictal drowsiness, a key discriminator from seizure activity.
The posturing is thought to be a reflexive or learned manoeuvre that relieves the discomfort of acid reflux or reduces oesophageal obstruction, rather than a primary neurological disorder.
It typically presents in infancy and early childhood and is over-represented in children with neurodisability, in whom reflux is common and communication limited.
Effective treatment of the underlying reflux — positional and feeding measures with acid suppression — usually abolishes the movements, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
Associated features may include feeding refusal, irritability, faltering growth, iron-deficiency anaemia and, occasionally, apparent apnoeic or brief resolved unexplained events.
Misdiagnosis as epilepsy, infantile spasms or a primary dystonia is common and frequently leads to unnecessary neurological investigation and antiepileptic exposure.
reference.pathophysiology: Sandifer syndrome is a movement phenomenon secondary to gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and sometimes hiatus hernia, rather than a disorder of the central nervous system. Acid or volume reflux into the distal oesophagus is thought to provoke discomfort and vagally mediated afferent stimulation, and the stereotyped extension and lateral flexion of the neck and trunk are believed to be a protective postural response that lengthens and straightens the oesophagus, reduces reflux, relieves pain and may safeguard the airway. Because the movements are reflexive and non-epileptic, the electroencephalogram is normal and awareness is retained; resolution of the reflux, whether through maturation of the lower oesophageal sphincter or with therapy, characteristically resolves the posturing.
additionalDifferentials: Epileptic seizures, including focal tonic seizures and infantile spasms
Benign paroxysmal torticollis of infancy and paroxysmal tonic upgaze
Primary dystonia, including dopa-responsive dystonia, and other movement disorders
Benign myoclonus of infancy and shuddering attacks
Congenital muscular torticollis due to sternocleidomastoid contracture
Drug-induced dystonic reactions, for example to antidopaminergic agents
Posterior fossa or cervical cord pathology and atlantoaxial instability
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis supported by a symptom diary or home video correlating episodes with feeds
Therapeutic trial of anti-reflux measures as a diagnostic-therapeutic step
Oesophageal pH and multichannel intraluminal impedance monitoring
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study to assess for hiatus hernia, malrotation or anatomical anomaly
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy where oesophagitis or eosinophilic oesophagitis is suspected
Electroencephalogram, typically normal, if seizures cannot be excluded clinically
Neuroimaging of brain and cervical spine if neurological signs or atypical features are present
redFlags: Altered awareness, cyanosis or apnoea during episodes, suggesting seizure or airway compromise
Faltering growth, persistent vomiting or haematemesis
Focal neurological signs, developmental regression or an abnormal interictal examination
Episodes unrelated to feeds or persisting despite adequate reflux treatment
Bilious vomiting raising concern for malrotation with volvulus
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; the condition is self-limiting and typically resolves with maturation of the lower oesophageal sphincter and control of reflux during infancy. When correctly identified and treated there are no long-term neurological sequelae.
pitfalls: Labelling episodes as epilepsy and starting antiepileptic drugs unnecessarily
Overlooking reflux because posturing rather than regurgitation dominates the presentation
Attributing the torticollis solely to a musculoskeletal cause
Failing to consider Sandifer syndrome in neurodisabled children in whom reflux is common
Stopping anti-reflux therapy prematurely before symptoms have resolved
references: NASPGHAN-ESPGHAN Pediatric Gastroesophageal Reflux Clinical Practice Guidelines
management: Treatment of the underlying gastro-oesophageal reflux as the definitive measure, with positional and feeding modifications such as upright positioning and thickened or smaller frequent feeds
Acid suppression with a proton pump inhibitor or H2-receptor antagonist to relieve the reflux driving the posturing
Surgical anti-reflux fundoplication reserved for refractory cases or where a significant hiatus hernia is present
Reassurance that the posturing is a benign, self-limiting reflux-related phenomenon that resolves with reflux control and sphincter maturation
Avoidance of unnecessary antiepileptic drugs by recognising the preserved consciousness and normal electroencephalogram
Symptom diary or home video monitoring to confirm the temporal link to feeds and response to therapy
Additional gastroenterology and multidisciplinary input for children with neurodisability in whom reflux is common
